text.en: Nita and Monu visit Ritu's house and get milk in different glasses. Who gets the most? Ritu's sister pours all the milk into three same-sized glasses and then we can see. In this chapter we learn how to find which holds more and which weighs more.

The amount a vessel can hold is called its capacity. We can compare two glasses by pouring from one to the other. If a small glass is filled and poured into a big glass, the big glass does not fill up. So it holds more. A jug holds more than a glass, and a glass holds more than a ladle. We can use a small vessel as a measure and count how many fill a bigger one. If 4 glasses fill a jug, then 8 glasses are needed for 2 jugs. The quantity of water stays the same when we pour it into different vessels.
A litre is a unit that we use to measure how much liquid a vessel holds. Milk is often measured in litres. A measuring cup is used to give 1 litre of milk, so everybody gets the same amount. A glass usually holds less than a litre, and a bucket holds more than a litre. Half a litre is exactly half of a litre, and a quarter litre is one of four equal parts of a litre. Two half-litre mugs make a litre, and four quarter-litre glasses make a litre. It takes about 5 litres of water to make a single plastic bottle of 1 litre. Using our own bottle saves water.
Some things are heavier and some are lighter. A pan balance helps to see which is heavier, because the heavier object makes its pan go down. We can weigh a pencil by balancing it with coins or erasers. A heavier object needs more of them. A matchbox filled with sand can be used as a weight for slightly heavier things such as a pencil box. A kilogram is a unit for weight. Sugar and salt are often sold in packets of 1 kilogram. A half-kilogram packet is half as heavy and a quarter-kilogram packet is one of four equal parts. Two half-kilogram packets balance one 1-kilogram packet on a pan balance.
Three balls look the same, but one is heavier. We place one ball on each pan, and keep the third aside. If the pans balance, the ball left aside is the heavy one. If one pan goes down, that pan holds the heavy ball. So one weighing is enough. To order three balls from lightest to heaviest we compare them two at a time on the pan balance.

Look at a tall, narrow cup and a short, wide cup. The taller water level gives you a clue about the shape of the cup. How could you check which cup holds more?
Fill the tall cup to the top and pour it carefully into the wide cup. If there is still space in the wide cup, the wide cup holds more.
If the wide cup fills exactly and no water is left, both cups hold the same amount. The shape can change while the capacity stays the same.
For a fair comparison, use the same small cup to fill each container. Fill the measuring cup to the same level every time.
Suppose a pot needs six equal cups of water and a jug needs four. The pot holds two cupfuls more.
A container can hold one litre when full even if there is very little water in it now. Capacity tells how much it can hold when it is full.

board.text: Capacity is how much it can hold

text.en: You need one litre for a recipe and have a half-litre mug and a quarter-litre cup. After one mugful, how many quarter-litre cupfuls do you still need?
You still need half a litre. Two equal quarters make a half, so add two quarter-litre cupfuls.
Check that the empty pans are level before you weigh anything. Then put the object on one pan and the weights on the other.
A large empty carton may be lighter than a small bag of rice. The pan that drops tells you which is heavier.
Imagine a bag balances exactly with one half-kilogram weight and one quarter-kilogram weight. How many quarter-kilogram weights would balance it?
A half-kilogram weight can be exchanged for two quarter-kilogram weights. Add the third quarter, and the pans will still balance.
Which unit would you use for milk in a jug and rice in a bag? Use litres to measure the liquid and kilograms to weigh the rice.

problem.en: Ritu's glass fills 3 small bowls. A jug fills 4 glasses. Which holds more, the jug or the glass?

text.en: One jug needs 4 glasses to fill.

why.en: A bigger vessel holds more small ones.

text.en: So the jug holds more than a glass.

problem.en: How many half-litre mugs fill a 1-litre bottle?

text.en: A half litre is half of a litre.
So 2 mugs fill the bottle.

problem.en: One of three balls is heavier. How can we find it with a single weighing?

text.en: Put one ball on each pan and keep one aside.

why.en: Two balls are compared and one is left out.

text.en: If the pans are level, the ball kept aside is the heavy one.

why.en: Equal pans mean the two on the pans are equal.

text.en: If one pan goes down, that pan holds the heavy ball.

prompt.en: Explain how you would find which of two glasses holds more.

requiredIdeas.en: If it overflows, the first holds more
If there is space left, the first holds less

commonMisconceptions.en: The taller glass always holds more
Weight and capacity mean the same

points.en: Capacity is how much a vessel can hold.
A litre is a unit for liquid. Two half litres or four quarter litres make a litre.
A pan balance shows which object is heavier, the lower pan.
A kilogram is a unit for weight. Two half kilograms make a kilogram.
One weighing is enough to find the heavier of three balls.
